# Title as claim enables traversal as reasoning

Don't name notes like topics ("thoughts on memory"). Name them like claims ("structure enables navigation without reading everything").

When you link to a claim-titled note, the link becomes part of your argument:

> "because *approvals guard against LLM mistakes not active attacks*, we can separate the security boundary from the approval UX"

The title IS the reasoning. Traversal IS thinking. The title functions as a typed signature — you know what you're getting before you load the full note. A topic label like "memory notes" is an undocumented function; a claim like "structure enables navigation" tells you the return value. This connects to how [types applied to documents mark affordances](./instructions-are-typed-callables.md) — a claim title is an affordance declaration.

## Prior work

Propositional titles are established practice in several fields:

- **Academic writing** — thesis statements and paper titles that state the conclusion. The abstract leads with the claim.
- **Journalism** — headlines state the finding ("Scientists discover X"), not the topic ("Research about Y").
- **Evergreen notes** (Matuschak) — explicitly advocates for note titles as complete propositions rather than topic labels.
- **Zettelkasten practice** — Luhmann used precise descriptive titles; the community has extensive discussion of atomicity and title quality.

The *traversal-as-reasoning* consequence — when titles are claims, link-following reads as argument — came to us via [arscontexta](../agent-memory-systems/reviews/arscontexta.md), which likely drew on these same traditions. The [Toulmin argumentation model](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/general_writing/academic_writing/historical_perspectives_on_argumentation/toulmin_argument.html) provides the formal structure behind the "since/because" link semantics this enables.

**TODO:** This survey is from the agent's training data, not systematic. Matuschak's writing on evergreen notes and Zettelkasten community resources on title conventions are worth ingesting.

## Why it works

Inline links carry richer relationship data than metadata fields. The prose surrounding a link encodes WHY the linked note matters here — "because [X]" is a causal claim, "since [Y]" is a foundation claim, "but [Z]" is a tension. Claim-as-title makes these constructions possible, because topic labels don't compose grammatically. You can write "since [claims must be specific enough to be wrong]" but not "since [specificity notes]." Our [link relationship semantics](../reference/adr/009-link-relationship-semantics.md) formalize this — argumentative links ("since", "because") and referential links ("see", "as defined in") are different intents that require different anchor context.

Progressive disclosure depends on this. The first disclosure layer is titles. If titles are claims, agents can curate what to load based on what each note argues. If titles are topics, agents must load notes to discover what they argue — the disclosure layer fails. This is why [instruction specificity should match loading frequency](./instruction-specificity-should-match-loading-frequency.md) — the loading hierarchy assumes that titles and descriptions carry enough signal for agents to decide what to load next.

**Practical benefits:**
- scanning file tree = scanning arguments
- following links = following reasoning chains
- the vault becomes readable without opening files

## Where it breaks: multi-claim documents

The pattern works best for ideas that ARE single claims. It breaks for **compositional documents** — specs, frameworks, classification systems — that embody multiple independent design choices.

[Collections and types](../reference/collections-and-types.md) is a clear example. It composes several facts: an artifact has separate collection and type contracts, `type:` is a path-valued identity, schemas and semantic review consume different parts of the type spec, and specs may be global or collection-local. Each fact could support a standalone claim note, but no single claim subsumes the whole operational account.

The traversal-as-reasoning framing explains why. A claim-titled note can serve as a premise: "since [X], therefore Y." A multi-claim document can't serve as a single premise because it IS multiple premises. When you write "see *document classification*," you're not invoking a reasoning step — you're pointing to a reference. The link semantics shift from argumentative ("since," "because") to referential ("see," "as defined in").

| Document kind | Title convention | Link semantics | Role in traversal |
|---|---|---|---|
| Single-claim (insight, rationale) | Claim title | "since [X]", "because [X]" | Premise in reasoning chain |
| Multi-claim (spec, framework) | Topical title | "see [X]", "as defined in [X]" | Reference, not premise |
| Definitional (term pinning) | The term itself | "see [X]", "[X] means..." | Reference, not premise |

**Definitional notes** are a second exception. Notes like [codification](./definitions/codification.md), [constraining](./definitions/constraining.md), and [context engineering](./definitions/context-engineering.md) pin down how a technical term is used in this project. Their titles are the terms they define — topical by nature. They function as reference entries: you link to them for precision ("as defined in [codification]"), not as premises in reasoning chains. Like specs, they can link TO claim-notes for justification while carrying topical titles themselves.

The two layers coexist. Specs link TO their constituent claim-notes for justification ([document types should be verifiable](./document-types-should-be-verifiable.md) is the rationale extracted from the classification spec). Claim-notes link TO specs as the system they support. But they have different title conventions because they play different roles in traversal.

This maps onto the existing type system: a claim-titled note may change to `type: theory/types/structured-claim.md` when its body meets that contract; ADRs, design proposals, generated indexes, and other multi-claim structural types carry topical titles. The title convention is independent of the type — an artifact using `type: types/note.md` can use a claim title.

## The shadow side

Not every idea decomposes into a single declarative sentence — some are relational, procedural, emergent, or compositional. When reformulation feels forced, the question is whether the insight isn't ready or the format can't accommodate it. The type system makes this explicit: a note can keep `type: types/note.md` with a topical title, and that's fine.

# Retained system-definition artifacts enable persistent deployment-time adaptation

[Continual learning requires governing behaviour-changing writes, not just storing content](./continual-learning-requires-governing-behaviour-changing-writes.md) argues that deployed systems need durable behavior changes installed within their operating feedback loops. These changes need not wait for another model-weight training cycle. During deployment, a system can evaluate and retain changes to [system-definition artifacts](./definitions/system-definition-artifact.md)—prompts, rules, tools, schemas, tests, and configuration that it consumes with binding force.

This is a distinct adaptation path because the selected change affects later sessions without becoming part of the model's weights. This note calls that path **deployment-time adaptation**. The process counts as learning when deployment experience drives a proposal, evaluation selects it, and retention allows it to change later behavior.

## Lifecycle phase is not update speed

Five properties must remain separate:

- **Lifecycle phase:** Whether the change is produced before or during deployment.
- **Update latency:** How long proposal, evaluation, and safe installation take.
- **Persistence:** Whether the selected change survives the run that produced it.
- **Update mechanism:** Weight training, context assembly, artifact revision, or another process.
- **[Representational form](./definitions/representational-form.md):** Whether the retained change lives in distributed model weights, natural language, symbolic code, or a mixture.

Common adaptation paths combine these properties in different ways, but they do not form exclusive timescale categories. Offline weight training is usually durable and occurs before deployment, yet online training can update weights during deployment. Live context changes behavior within a session, but context alone does not write changes into later sessions. Summaries or saved state persist only because another retention path stores them. A system-definition edit can be produced within one session and retained for later ones. When an evidence-responsive selection loop completes this artifact-revision path within the deployed system's operating cadence, the result is persistent deployment-time adaptation. “During deployment” locates the change in the lifecycle; it does not by itself make the change fast.

## Why localized artifacts are practical now

Localized, versioned artifacts can make a deployment-time change inspectable, diffable, selectively revisable, and rollbackable. This advantage is conditional rather than intrinsic. A global natural-language policy can have an open-ended behavioral surface, while a routed parameter adapter can be tightly confined. Validation becomes more tractable only when the artifact's actual authority and dependency neighborhood bound the consequences that must be checked, as developed by [the readable-artifact loop](./readable-artifact-loop-is-the-tractable-unit-for-continual-learning.md).

Timing and form are therefore orthogonal. Parametric methods can also learn from deployment interaction. [OpenClaw-RL](../sources/openclaw-rl-train-any-agent-simply-by-talking.ingest.md) converts live next-state signals into rewards and token-level supervision for one policy through decoupled serving and training loops. The retained source does not establish when trained checkpoints enter serving, persist, pass acceptance validation, or roll back. It therefore grounds interaction-driven policy training during deployment, not a safe in-place weight-update lifecycle. Readable artifacts are useful where their explicit operational boundaries make evaluation and rollback cheaper; they do not exclusively occupy the deployment-time category.

Artifact libraries can also accumulate more behavior-shaping state than a single call can hold. Each call remains bounded by the [context-scarcity constraint](./context-efficiency-is-the-central-design-concern-in-agent-systems.md). This note treats progressive disclosure, skill routing, and retrieval as candidate mechanisms for selecting a relevant subset of retained artifacts into each call; that mechanism is an architectural inference here, not a result established by the linked note. It lets the deployed system retain more state over time without enlarging any individual context window or claiming parity with the breadth of a weight update.

## Why this is system learning

Herbert Simon's capacity-change criterion, stated in [learning is not only about generality](./learning-is-not-only-about-generality.md), treats a more or less permanent change in a system's capacity to adapt as learning. The relevant unit is [the deployed system, not the model alone](./the-deployed-system-not-the-model-is-the-unit-of-learning.md), because prompts, retrieval, tools, validators, and runtime policy jointly determine behavior.

Persistence alone is insufficient. A manually edited configuration remains an engineering input unless an evidence-responsive process evaluates and incorporates it. [A proposal-selection improvement loop requires search, evaluation, and operative retention](./a-proposal-selection-loop-requires-search-evaluation-and-retention.md); these operations distinguish learning from arbitrary durable maintenance. A human may still propose or approve the selected change. What matters is that deployment evidence bears on its selection and that the retained result affects later executions.

[Humanlaya's reported quality-system comparison (§5.4; snapshot required)](../sources/last-ai-built-by-humans-recursive-self-improvement.ingest.md) supplies a bounded example. Production feedback drives versioned changes to rules, prompts, examples, and skills; held-out checks and human review govern promotion into later batches. After four updates, V0 and V4 were compared on 600 packages excluded from updating, with the base model, tools, and processing budget unchanged. Packages with key defects after automated repair fell from 9.0% to 3.7%, and average human handling fell from 48 to 27 minutes per task. These company-reported results concern the whole revised quality system; they do not isolate individual edits or establish superiority over other adaptation mechanisms.

## Forms can coevolve

Deployment-time adaptation does not privilege natural language or code. [Constraining during deployment can produce learning outside weights](./constraining-during-deployment-can-produce-learning-outside-weights.md) develops one concrete path in which prompts, schemas, tools, tests, and code accumulate adaptive capacity. Settled interpretations can move toward symbolic enforcement, while new evidence can reopen a commitment for model judgment. The allocation of state among natural-language, symbolic, and distributed-parametric forms may therefore change while the timing and persistence of the learning loop remain the same. How those forms should divide responsibility is the separate argument in [treat continual learning as representational-form coevolution](./treat-continual-learning-as-representational-form-coevolution.md).

## Boundary

The claim is that a persistent deployment-time adaptation path exists outside model-weight updates—not that it is a third exhaustive timescale, always faster than training, or exclusive to readable artifacts. Its practical advantage depends on evidence-responsive selection and a validation surface whose consequences are actually bounded.

# Link graph plus timestamps enables make-like staleness detection

Notes that reference current design state go stale when that state changes. A note proposing changes to WRITING.md becomes misleading once WRITING.md adopts those changes. Currently there is no mechanism to detect this — staleness is discovered only when someone happens to re-read the note.

## The make analogy

`make` solves a structurally similar problem: source files change, and downstream targets need rebuilding. It tracks dependencies between files and compares timestamps. If a source is newer than its target, the target is rebuilt.

A KB note that links to another file is making a claim about that file's state. If the target changes, the claim may be stale. The link graph already encodes the dependency; git provides the timestamps. No new annotation is needed.

## Mechanism

1. Walk the link graph to extract each note's outbound links.
2. For each link target, compare the note's last-modified time (git log) against the target's last-modified time.
3. If any target is newer than the note, flag the note for review.

The "rebuild" is not automatic rewriting — it's a review prompt. A human or agent checks whether the change to the target invalidates what the note says about it. This is analogous to `make` invoking a recipe, except the recipe is "re-read and decide."

## False positives and filtering

Not every change to a target invalidates the linking note. WRITING.md might get a typo fix that doesn't affect any note referencing it. This is the same tradeoff `make` accepts — it rebuilds targets that may not need rebuilding because the cost of a redundant rebuild is lower than the cost of a missed one.

For a KB, the cost of a false positive is "agent re-reads a note unnecessarily." That's cheap. A false negative can leave an apparently complete navigation artifact suppressing fallback discovery — the problem [indexes lower recall when they suppress retrieval that would find more](./indexes-lower-recall-when-they-suppress-retrieval-that-would-find-more.md) identifies.

Possible filters to reduce noise:
- Only flag notes whose targets changed substantively (exclude commits that only touch whitespace or frontmatter).
- Prioritize links whose accompanying claims depend on the target's current design state over links used only for navigation.
- Weight by note centrality — high-centrality stale notes are higher priority.

## Scope

This works for intra-KB links where both files are in git. It does not cover external references (URLs, API docs) — those need a different mechanism (periodic link checking, `last-checked` fields as [related-systems reviews](../agent-memory-systems/README.md) already use).

## Relationship to existing staleness work

The KB already has staleness concepts:
- [Indexes lower recall when they suppress retrieval that would find more](./indexes-lower-recall-when-they-suppress-retrieval-that-would-find-more.md) identifies the fallback-suppression failure that makes some stale navigation dangerous.
- [Quality signals for KB evaluation](./quality-signals-for-kb-evaluation.md) proposes note-age-vs-connection-count as a staleness proxy.
- Related-system reviews use `last-checked` for external sources.

This note adds a dependency-aware mechanism that is more precise than age-based heuristics: a note modified yesterday can be stale if its target was modified today.

## What would defeat this claim?

If most staleness comes from notes whose claims drift due to accumulated context changes across many files (rather than specific target changes), then pairwise timestamp comparison would miss the important cases. The mechanism assumes staleness is traceable to specific linked targets. [High-explanatory-reach revisions](./brainstorming-how-explanatory-reach-informs-kb-design.md) are the specific mechanism that produces this failure mode — revising a foundational principle may touch few files directly while silently invalidating downstream reasoning across many notes.

# Near-decomposability may make local inspection affordable

An artifact may be affordable to inspect when the question can be answered by reading one part and summaries of its interactions with the rest. A division whose parts interact weakly enough for this is a near-decomposition. This note conjectures that knowing such a division can make local inspection affordable. It also conjectures the converse: every inspector whose budget is smaller than the artifact needs such a division, at a granularity set by its budget and question.

The proposal applies to three sources of [opacity](./opacity-depends-on-the-inspection-question-and-budget.md), where answering the question exceeds the inspection budget: scale, the reference's form, and deliberate obfuscation. It transfers Herbert Simon's account of dynamic systems to dependencies within artifacts; that transfer is this note's conjecture, not Simon's claim. Description length is explored as a proxy for the amount to explain. Finding and checking the explanation also cost work.

## The condition

Simon's [Architecture of Complexity](../sources/herbert-simon-architecture-of-complexity.ingest.md) introduces the condition as a second approximation after perfectly separable systems: a theory of nearly decomposable systems, in which the interactions, verbatim, "among the subsystems are weak, but not negligible." Two propositions follow, quoted verbatim with the capture's typography: "( a ) in a nearly decomposable system, the shortrun behavior of each of the component subsystems is approximately independent of the short-run behavior of the other components; ( b ) in the long run, the behavior of any one of the components depends in only an aggregate way on the behavior of the other components."

The proposed transfer reads interaction as dependency between the units of an artifact: a call, a citation, a shared variable, a weight that two computations use. If the question's relevant dependencies fit inside one block and the remaining effects can be captured by interface summaries, local inspection need not read the whole artifact. The block and those summaries determine how much material must be examined. Whether that material is affordable to understand and check is a further question.

Dense coupling, or a hub every block depends on, can defeat local reading while each unit stays readable.

In this transfer, the horizon and tolerance determine which interactions may be ignored or summarized. A decomposition useful for one question need not support another. The analogy does not establish that every artifact has a short horizon on which questions localize, or that every long-horizon question reaches every block.

## A proposed description-length proxy

The proposed proxy for inspection cost follows [Grünwald's](../sources/grunwald-mdl-tutorial.ingest.md) crude two-part form of the minimum description length principle, verbatim: "The best point hypothesis H ∈ H(1) ∪ H(2) ∪ . . . to explain the data D is the one which minimizes the sum L(H) + L(D|H), where • L(H) is the length, in bits, of the description of the hypothesis; and • L(D|H) is the length, in bits, of the description of the data when encoded with the help of the hypothesis."

Mapped to inspection, the hypothesis is the block and its rules, and the residual is what the aggregates and the exceptions add. In the [prompt case](./english-can-approximate-a-model-defined-prompt-language.md), the hypothesis is the coarse English account and the residual describes observed behavior left unexplained by it. The proposed empirical test probes that residual; a description-length score additionally requires a specified encoding.

The measure is relative to a description method. [Grünwald](../sources/grunwald-mdl-tutorial.ingest.md) requires one that is, verbatim, "restrictive enough" that the shortest description is computable, chosen by prior knowledge of the domain. For inspection, the description method is the vocabulary of units the consumption path exposes. The same artifact therefore has different costs under different paths: opacity is path-relative.

A found explanation and its residual supply an upper bound on the shortest description available in the chosen description method. The restriction quoted above makes the minimum computable in practical MDL; a search that merely retains the shortest explanation found so far need not have reached it. Neither quantity bounds the effort of finding or checking that explanation without a further cost model. Description length is a proposed proxy for the amount to explain, not a measure of that work. No calibrated relation between these costs is established here.

The hypothesis side can be gamed. [Grünwald](../sources/grunwald-mdl-tutorial.ingest.md) notes, verbatim, that the length of a hypothesis "can be very large under one code, but quite short under another", so a crude code for hypotheses is "in danger of becoming arbitrary". A comparison of inspection costs is honest only when the vocabulary of units is fixed before the comparison. The KB computes neither description length nor the work of finding or checking an explanation. The proposed proxy fixes what a cost comparison has to hold constant.

## One failure, three sources

The conjecture reads the three sources of opacity as different obstacles to local decomposition:

- **Scale.** A decomposition is known, and the block containing the question is too large to read, or a hub couples it to everything. Each unit is readable; the question is not affordable.
- **The reference's form.** The units exposed by the reference may not align with the question. Kernels and tensor operands expose runtime operations without supplying a readable instruction-level rule. A coarse semantic description of the prompt may still answer the question, as [the English approximation account](./english-can-approximate-a-model-defined-prompt-language.md) explains. Opacity remains where that description is insufficient and the relevant detail cannot be established affordably; the absence of a separate parameter block alone does not establish it.
- **Deliberate obfuscation.** A transformation may hide or disrupt a decomposition while preserving the function. Whether this explains the inspection obstacle must be established for the transformation and question. The cryptographic results summarized in the opacity note do not by themselves establish this structural account.

Known but expensive, unknown, and disrupted would then be three states of one obstacle. Opacity's definition does not depend on this unification succeeding.

## A necessity conjecture

The sections above conjecture sufficiency. This section conjectures necessity, as a universal claim. An inspector whose budget is smaller than the artifact must answer from one part plus summaries of the rest. Its answer is correct within the question's tolerance only if the omitted interactions can be summarized within that tolerance. That is a near-decomposition relative to the question. The need follows from the budget bound, not from the kind of inspector: a person, a model call and a program analyzer face it alike.

An inspector with an unlimited budget is the limiting case, not a counterexample. Laplace's demon, which tracks every particle, needs no summaries. A demon able to track every molecule in a glass of water, but no more, still needs aggregates such as temperature for the ocean around the glass.

The conjecture's main use is diagnostic. An argument that some inspector needs no aggregate concepts assumes that its budget is at least as large as the system it inspects. A thought experiment can leave that premise unstated. Stating it shows that the conclusion holds only for the limiting case, and that a larger budget moves the level at which aggregates become necessary without removing the need.

**Granularity and partition.** For one artifact and one question, inspectors with different budgets differ in granularity. A larger budget allows a larger block, a longer horizon or a tighter tolerance. A smaller budget forces smaller blocks and coarser summaries, which succeed only where the question tolerates them. A different question can make different interactions matter. It then changes the partition itself, not only its fineness, which is why a decomposition useful for one question need not support another. The conjecture is that some near-decomposition is always needed, not that one partition serves every inspector.

**Certificates and abstraction.** A certificate check appears to answer a question without decomposing the artifact. This note's argument is that the check moves the need to a different artifact. Checking a certificate is local reading of the certificate: each step is checked against a few others. The certificate is built to be nearly decomposable for the checking question. An abstraction moves the need the same way: it is read in parts, and it serves only where it summarizes the omitted interactions within the question's tolerance. This argument gives a conjectured answer to the third open question below; it does not close it. An affordable inspection method that reads no artifact locally would refute it.

**Need does not imply availability.** The conjecture states what affordable inspection requires, not that the requirement can be met. Where no near-decomposition exists at the granularity an inspector can afford, the artifact is opaque to that inspector for that question. An artifact without one therefore does not refute the conjecture; an affordable correct answer obtained without one would. How often the requirement is met is the selection-effect question under Scope.

## Finding an intervention point does not establish safe repair

Mechanistic interpretability is the search for a decomposition where none is exposed. [Templeton and co-authors](../sources/scaling-monosemanticity-claude-3-sonnet.ingest.md) train sparse autoencoders on a production model's activations and test the found units by intervention. Clamping the Golden Gate Bridge feature to ten times its maximum activation changes behavior as the feature's interpretation predicts; verbatim, "In this example, the model starts to self-identify as the Golden Gate Bridge!"

Under the path that addresses features, the activations are localized for the behaviors the found features cover, and [the authors](../sources/scaling-monosemanticity-claude-3-sonnet.ingest.md) are explicit that the coverage is partial. Verbatim, they "could only find features corresponding to about 60% of the boroughs" of London in their largest dictionary, and call the found set "an incomplete description of the model's internal representations". So localization under an interpretability path is graded by coverage, and the form under the path on which a system runs the model is unchanged.

[ROME](../sources/rome-locating-and-editing-factual-associations-in-gpt.ingest.md) is the same move on weights: a factual association is located, edited, and the edit's effect checked.

Finding an interpretable feature provides a place to intervene. It does not establish that the intervention preserves properties the system relies on. Even weak interactions can break a required invariant: an effect small enough to ignore when predicting typical behavior may be decisive when checking correctness.

The Golden Gate Bridge intervention demonstrates behavioral influence. It does not establish coupling strength or, without a stated requirement, an invariant violation. To assess whether a decomposition supports a particular repair, we must check whether its interaction summaries capture the effects relevant to the invariants that repair must preserve.

## Consequence for addressability

The proposed transfer to repair concerns how much must be checked after an edit. If a decomposition captures the dependencies relevant to the test, weak interactions across its blocks may let the inspector assess the edit within one block and its interfaces. Establishing that the decomposition captures those dependencies is part of the work.

That checking cost is separate from locating a repair candidate in an [addressable theory](./definitions/addressable-theory.md), whose parts can be inspected and revised individually. Locating a candidate and establishing that its repair preserves required invariants are separate achievements.

Consider a shared conversion routine that adds one where its stated rule requires adding two. A trace through that operation can identify a candidate fault even when many callers depend on the routine. Repairing it still requires checking the affected callers. Many callers establish a broad dependency footprint, not by themselves strong interaction between blocks.

For a direct coupled case, consider the explicitly stated equations `x = y + 1` and `y = 2x`: each equation is separately editable although changing either can change both variables. Separate editability does not require independent consequences.

## Scope

- Simon's result is a theorem about linear dynamic systems described by a nearly decomposable interaction matrix. Reading interaction as dependency between an artifact's units is this note's transfer. It needs a worked case on a real codebase or KB dependency graph before it can enter a definition as more than a mechanism.
- Decomposability is a structure. Opacity is a cost judgment on top of it, relative to the question, to the decompositions known, and to the budget. Composing a model from understood numerical operations does not by itself supply an affordable instruction-level description. A coarse semantic decomposition may supply one without locating separate parameter blocks.
- Simon flags a selection effect: a world may look hierarchic because its non-hierarchic parts elude understanding. The mechanism explains the affordable cases without showing that they predominate. Under the necessity conjecture, the same effect is expected: artifacts without an affordable near-decomposition are the ones that stay opaque, so the affordable cases studied will all be nearly decomposable.
- The necessity argument is close to definitional once a summary correct within tolerance is read as a near-decomposition. That limits what it can predict, not its diagnostic use of exposing an unstated unbounded-budget premise. Its empirical content lies in whether certificates, abstractions and execution-based evidence fit that reading. No such case has been worked through.

## Open Questions

- Compression. Simon ties near-decomposability to the redundancy that makes a compact description of a system possible, and the [epiplexity](../sources/from-entropy-to-epiplexity-rethinking-information-computational.ingest.md) ingest's time-bounded description length is the nearest formal neighbor. Whether inspection cost and compressibility are one quantity or two is a separate task.
- Whether obfuscation is exactly the destruction of near-decomposability, or only one route to it.
- Whether affordable abstraction or certificate checking can answer a question without any near-decomposition. The necessity conjecture answers no, by moving the need to the certificate or abstraction. A worked certificate scheme would test that answer.
- Whether execution-based evidence is local reading. Running an artifact and reading its outputs inspects a trace, not the artifact. Whether sampled behavior answers a question or only bounds it decides whether execution can refute the necessity conjecture.
- The worked case named under Scope.

# Agent statelessness makes routing architectural, not learned

A human developer who works in a knowledge base gradually builds intuition: "for this kind of task, look here." They learn which wiki page covers authentication, which convention governs naming, which template fits a design note. Eventually they navigate without conscious effort.

An LLM agent never does this. Each session starts cold. It cannot learn "last time I needed the structured-claim template, I found it in `theory/types/`." It cannot develop a hunch that a relevant skill might exist. Every session is day one.

This means every mechanism that directs the agent to the right knowledge at the right time — routing tables, skill descriptions, type templates, naming conventions, directory structure, activation triggers, area indexes — is permanent architecture. For a human, these are conveniences you outgrow. For an agent, they're prosthetics you never stop needing.

The [methodology enforcement](./methodology-enforcement-is-constraining.md) gradient describes practices hardening from instruction → skill → hook → script. The *practices* mature. The *agent* stays exactly as raw as it was on day one. This asymmetry is the core of the note: the system learns, the agent doesn't.

## Progressive disclosure replaces navigation intuition

A human holds an approximate mental model of the whole knowledge base. An agent can only hold what's loaded. Since [context efficiency is the central design concern](./context-efficiency-is-the-central-design-concern-in-agent-systems.md), you can't load everything — so you must route to the right layer at the right time. In this KB, the loading hierarchy is our concrete progressive disclosure system:

1. **CLAUDE.md** loads unconditionally — the agent always knows where to route
2. **Skill descriptions** load cheaply — the agent decides whether to load the full skill
3. **Skill bodies** load on activation — imperative instructions for the current task
4. **Type templates** load per directory — structural guidance matching the destination
5. **Methodology notes** load on demand — deep reasoning for edge cases

Each layer filters what the agent needs to consider, and each layer must route correctly to the next. A gap at any level creates unreachable knowledge.

## The degradation cliff

When a human encounters a situation their routing aids don't cover, they reason from experience — slower, less confident, but adequate. They notice "something feels off" and search more broadly.

An agent has no equivalent signal. When its loaded context doesn't cover a situation, it falls back on training — which may have no relationship to the KB's methodology. It doesn't degrade into "the same agent, but less certain." It degrades into a *different* system — a generic LLM rather than a KB-augmented one. The human system degrades along a continuum: expert → competent → novice → uncertain. The agent system has a cliff: KB-augmented → generic.

This makes every omission in routing infrastructure dangerous. A routing table missing an entry means the agent doesn't know the destination exists. A skill omitting edge-case reasoning produces confident execution with systematic errors. A naming convention not followed makes the note unfindable. The agent executes confidently within whatever scope is loaded, unaware of what wasn't routed to it.

## Source vs. compiled

The cliff creates a maintenance discipline: routing artifacts must stay in sync with methodology, because the agent can't bridge the gap when they drift apart.

Methodology notes are source code. Skills, routing tables, type templates, and naming conventions are compiled artifacts. You maintain the source (read methodology when revising routing); you ship the binary (load routing artifacts at runtime). The [instruction specificity principle](./instruction-specificity-should-match-loading-frequency.md) says "match instruction specificity to loading frequency." Agent statelessness explains *why* this is load-bearing: the agent cannot compensate for missing specificity by drawing on remembered methodology. If the specific routing isn't loaded, it doesn't exist.

The two genres have structurally different quality criteria. Source can be exploratory, tentative, argumentative — it's for reasoning. Compiled artifacts must be imperative, complete, unambiguous — they're for execution. The methodology reader has rich context and time to deliberate; the routing consumer has limited context and must act. The agent isn't a learner; it's a runtime. The KB isn't a curriculum; it's a deployment environment. (The [human-LLM differences](./human-llm-differences-are-load-bearing-for-knowledge-system-design.md) note develops why both pedagogical and purely mechanistic metaphors mislead here.)

## Design consequences

Three requirements follow:

1. **Engineering discipline.** Routing infrastructure needs the same treatment as production code — versioned, tested, reviewed.
2. **Staleness detection.** When methodology changes, routing artifacts derived from it silently drift. The agent has no "that doesn't seem right" intuition to catch it. Some mechanism — diffing, periodic audit, dependency tracking — must detect when compiled routing has diverged from its source.
3. **Behavioral completeness.** Each routing artifact must include enough reasoning for edge cases and explicit boundaries so the agent recognizes when it's outside scope. Partial routing produces confident execution with systematic errors — worse than no routing at all.

Persistent memory across sessions would relax the statelessness assumption, but routing scales with the knowledge base itself. Even an agent that remembers where it found things last time faces a navigation problem proportional to KB size.

# Mocking the tool boundary makes instruction behavior testable in isolation

When an LLM instruction uses tools to read, search or modify external state,
replacing those tools with controlled responses lets a test fix what the agent
encounters and capture what it attempts. The test can check execution behavior
that is not recoverable from the final artifact alone.

This tests the instruction's execution, not just its output: [a satisfactory
artifact does not establish a reliable generator](./programming-practices-for-prompts-need-question-specific-evidence.md).
The expected behavior must come from the [applicable requirement](./prompting-changes-failure-diagnosis-with-the-semantic-reference.md),
not merely reproduce what an earlier run happened to do.

## Example: discovery without source modification

Suppose an instruction must find connections among notes and write a report,
without modifying the source notes. A test supplies a target and candidate notes
through controlled reads and searches, and captures attempted writes.

The agent might produce a convincing report while also attempting to rewrite a
source note. Checking the report alone would miss that violation. Capturing the
attempted effects exposes it, even when the mock prevents the actual change.

The test must cover every available mutation route. Checking that no editing
tool was called is insufficient if a shell or another write tool can change the
same files. An unobserved route is a gap in the isolation claim.

## What the checks establish

A captured trace can support deterministic checks such as whether an attempted
write targeted a protected source. Output structure can also be checked
mechanically. Whether a reported connection is justified usually needs semantic
judgment; a required name appearing in the report does not establish that
judgment.

A deterministic assertion does not make the agent's behavior deterministic.
Repeated runs can expose variation under the recorded conditions, but passing
the tested cases does not establish compliance on untested inputs.

## Scope

Mocking tests behavior against the simulated environment. A canned search result
can test how the agent uses that result; it cannot establish that a real search
implementation would return it. The mock must preserve the behavior relevant to
the failure being tested.

Mocking is one route to controlled execution, not a requirement for all
instruction tests. Real tools operating on an isolated temporary corpus can
support other checks. Neither route by itself demonstrates correctness in the
production environment.

## Open Questions

- Which tool behaviors must a mock preserve for failures found in isolation to
  remain relevant under real execution?

# Mechanistic constraints make Popperian KB recommendations actionable

This note tries to apply Popperian epistemology — conjecture and refutation — to KB design. It asks whether the KB's computational constraints (bounded context, underspecification, statelessness) give Popperian practices concrete value here, and derives three specific practices from the analysis.

## Why conjecture is forced, not chosen

[An instruction permits a set of behaviors and the executor produces one](./prompting-changes-failure-diagnosis-with-the-semantic-reference.md), so every agent run selects among the readings the instruction permits. That selection is an implicit hypothesis about what the instruction means in this context. The agent conjectures whether it wants to or not.

This is distinct from claim-level conjecture. A claim-titled note is an object-level proposition ("context efficiency is the central design concern"). A runtime interpretation is an execution-level guess about intent ("the user probably wants me to add a link here, not rewrite the section"). Both are criticizable, but they live at different levels and need different criticism mechanisms:

- **Claims** need explicit falsifiers — conditions stated in the note itself that would invalidate the claim.
- **Interpretations** need capture-on-rejection — when a user corrects "that's not what I meant," the correction should become a durable test case, not a forgotten conversation turn.

## Why criticism must be structural, not ambient

You might think the LLM can just "notice" when claims conflict or interpretations fail. Two constraints prevent this:

[LLM context is composed without scoping](./llm-context-is-composed-without-scoping.md) — unstructured accumulation causes interference. Contradictions between notes loaded into the same context aren't flagged; they're silently averaged. [Context efficiency is the central design concern](./context-efficiency-is-the-central-design-concern-in-agent-systems.md) — we cannot load everything and let the model sort it out. So criticism that depends on loading two contradictory notes simultaneously is unreliable.

This means criticism must be externalized into the notes themselves. Claim titles and [link semantics](../tags/links-README.md) already do part of this — [title as claim enables traversal as reasoning](./title-as-claim-enables-traversal-as-reasoning.md), and typed links make foundation/extension/contradiction explicit. But the current system lacks two things: a way to state what would *defeat* a claim, and a systematic pass that looks for contradiction before looking for agreement.

## Whether criticism can converge depends on oracle quality

Not all criticism is useful. [Error correction works with above-chance oracles and decorrelated checks](./error-correction-works-above-chance-oracles-with-decorrelated-checks.md) — criticism converges only when the checking process is better than random and independent of the original error. An LLM re-reading its own note under the same prompt is a correlated check and will not reliably find flaws. A human reviewer, a different prompt strategy, or a structural test (does the falsifier condition hold?) provides decorrelated checking.

This is why falsifier blocks work: they convert criticism from "re-read and see if it still seems right" (correlated, weak) into "check whether this specific condition has been observed" (decorrelated, testable).

## Proposed practices

<!-- Each proposal below should be deleted and replaced with a link to its
     landing place (WRITING.md, skill spec, etc.) once adopted. When all
     proposals are adopted this section can be removed entirely. -->

- **Falsifier blocks on claim notes** — Add a short "What would defeat this claim?" block to `note` and `structured-claim` types. The attempt to write one is diagnostic — if you cannot state what would refute a claim, that reveals something about the claim's nature (definitional? tautological? too vague to test?). Not every claim has a clean falsifier, and that's fine. The value is in the attempt, not universal coverage. Target: `kb/instructions/WRITING.md` templates.

- **Contradiction-first connection passes** — When `/connect` discovers relationships, it should look for tension and contradiction *before* looking for agreement and extension. The current default is to find notes that "extend" or "ground" the new note. Reversing the priority means criticism is not optional — every note gets at least one check for conflict with existing claims. Target: `/connect` skill.

- **Rejected interpretations become instruction tests** — When a user corrects an agent's interpretation ("that's not what I meant"), that rejection is evidence about the instruction's ambiguity. Encoding the rejected case as a test or example in the instruction makes the same failure harder to repeat. This is [constraining](./definitions/constraining.md) driven by error, and across sessions it compounds as [deploy-time learning](./retained-artifacts-enable-persistent-deployment-time-adaptation.md). Target: workflow convention or hook.

## What would defeat this claim?

If bounded-context systems could reliably detect contradictions without externalized structure — e.g. through improved retrieval that always surfaces conflicting notes together — then the "criticism must be structural" argument weakens. The practices might still be useful, but the argument that KB mechanics *force* them would no longer hold.

# Title as claim makes overlap between notes visible

When two notes in an index have claim titles, overlap is immediately apparent:

- "prompt refinement is cleaner for the callee"
- "conversation pollutes callee context with misframing"

These are clearly arguing the same thing from different angles. A maintainer scanning the index can spot the overlap without opening either file. With topical titles ("agent communication patterns", "sub-agent coordination"), the overlap is invisible until you read both notes.

This matters because note proliferation is the default failure mode of a growing KB. Every new note risks duplicating an existing claim under different words. Claim titles turn overlap detection into a scanning task (cheap) rather than a reading task (expensive). The maintainer's question shifts from "what does this note argue?" to "is this claim already made elsewhere?" — and the answer is visible in the index.

The benefit compounds with index size. An index of 10 topical titles might hide overlap that's manageable. An index of 40 topical titles almost certainly hides overlap that's invisible. An index of 40 claim titles makes that overlap scannable.

# Use tests a decomposition locally; retained rationale is what makes transfer testable

A decomposition — a split of a system, task, or corpus into parts with boundaries between them — gets validated by being used. The modules compose, the sub-agents finish the task, each piece fits its context window. That is real evidence for exactly one proposition: this split sufficed in the context that produced it. It is [an outcome check, and an outcome check licenses replay rather than a rule](./checked-outcome-licenses-episode-retention-not-abstraction.md). What a designer usually wants from a working decomposition is a rule — *split on this seam* — and that is a transfer claim about other contexts, which use never touched.

That note leaves open where the process evidence would come from. For a runtime trace the intermediate steps happened and can be inspected. A decomposition's process is the design reasoning, and it leaves no residue in the product: the boundaries are visible, the forces they answer are not. Many different force-sets are consistent with the same split, so inspecting the artifact cannot recover which one was operative — design-rationale methods exist for precisely this gap, IDEF6 capturing rationale where constraints do not determine a unique decision ([how Commonplace distributes rationale records](../reference/design-rationale-management.md)). Hence *retained*: recording the rationale while the design reasoning is available leaves an antecedent that can be tested independently. Guided work with a current theory-holder can transfer situated understanding, but by itself leaves no durable record.

## Local success barely discriminates

Use exercises a conjunction — these boundaries *and* this context — and reports one bit about the whole. The set of decompositions that pass is therefore large: a boundary that answers nothing, an over-split, a seam imported by habit from another system, all survive as long as they are not actively harmful. So local success fails to separate load-bearing boundaries from inert ones, and that separation is the whole of transfer. What carries to a new context is a boundary answering a force that is also present there.

Parnas's KWIC example is the clean demonstration: two modularizations of the same small indexing program, both working, both producing the same output, differing in whether module boundaries hide the decisions likely to change. Running either discriminates them not at all. The difference appears only under change and reuse — the transfer cases — and what predicts it is the criterion, not the module list the criterion produced.

## What a rationale must contain for the transfer claim to have an antecedent

A transfer claim is conditional: this split works where such-and-such holds. A conditional is testable only through its antecedent, and rationale supplies it by recording, per boundary, which of three things the boundary answers:

- an **inherited constraint** — what the substrate or consumer forced (an effective context bound, a tool surface, a review budget);
- a **local requirement** — what this problem needed and another might not;
- a **free choice** — what was underdetermined and settled by convenience.

With that split recorded, a new context is checkable before anything is rebuilt: do the constraints still bind, are the local requirements present, and which parts were never load-bearing at all. Without it the only available move is to rebuild and see — another local test, not a test of the transfer claim. The effect of retention is not that transfer succeeds more often; it is that "this transfers" moves from untestable to testable. This is the condition clause that [abstracting an experience into a lesson requires](./abstract-an-experience-only-when-you-can-state-the-boundary.md), supplied for the case where the episode is a design act rather than a trace, and it is why [the why is the part that carries past the original case](./first-principles-reasoning-selects-for-explanatory-reach-over.md).

## Retained-but-unfaithful is worse than absent

Post-hoc rationalization is the standing failure, and the risk that makes [a misleading rationale worse than none when repair relies on it](./revision-guided-by-rationale-needs-faithfulness-not-just-legibility.md) also applies when transfer assessment relies on a recorded rationale. With no rationale, the transfer claim is untestable and visibly so; with a plausible but wrong one, the check runs against the stated force, passes, and the force that actually carried the local success is never examined. Retention makes the transfer claim testable; it does not make the test sound. What separates the two is intervention rather than reading — vary the stated force and see whether the decomposition's fit actually degrades.

## The claim's force scales with underdetermination

Change the premise and the conclusion moves. Where the problem determines the split — a protocol boundary, a hard data dependency, a transaction the external system will not let you straddle — the rationale is recoverable from the problem statement, retention buys little, and use approximates a test of the seam because there was nothing to choose. The gap this note names is proportional to how many alternative splits would also have worked locally, which is why it bites hardest on architecture and agent-team decomposition and barely at all on forced seams.

Repeated use across *varied* contexts is the other route, and it genuinely tests transfer — extensionally. Each new context that works narrows the region empirically. But it costs one full rebuild per sample and yields a list of contexts where the split held, never a statement of which feature carried, so it cannot answer the counterfactual (would this still hold if the review budget tripled?). Retained rationale is the intensional substitute for a sample nobody can afford.

## Nothing here is specific to splitting

The argument used three things: use exercises the whole configuration at once, the product underdetermines the reasons behind it, and a conditional needs its antecedent to be testable. Those hold for any design decision whose alternatives are discarded at design time — naming schemes, schema shapes, retrieval strategies, where a review gate sits. Decomposition is the sharpest instance because its discarded alternatives are maximally invisible: a working system displays its boundaries and never its rejected ones, so the artifact positively looks like its own justification.

## Scope

- The claim is about testability, not success. A complete and faithful rationale can describe a decomposition that transfers badly; it buys a test, not a result.
- A durable rationale is needed when a transfer claim must remain independently testable without its producing context. Within the session that produced the split the rationale is still in context, and the requirement is invisible there, which is part of why it gets skipped. The default-off rate is measurable: auditing this repository's own architecture decision records before requiring an alternatives section found 4 of 56 carrying alternatives prose, and none carrying it as a heading ([ADR 056](../reference/adr/056-adopted-and-retired-proposals-archive-out-of-the-frontier.md)).
- The maintenance cost is unmeasured: rationale drifts as the decomposition is refactored, and drifted rationale is unfaithful rationale. Whether faithful retention stays cheaper than the extensional route at library scale is open.

# Code and prompts can share a unified interface so programmers choose between them as systems evolve

Code functions and prompt-backed agents do not need separate invocation surfaces. A caller can use the same name, arguments, and result format—and an LLM caller can see the same operation description—whether a prompt or a function handles the call. That extends **information hiding** across the boundary between code and prompts: the interface tells callers how to invoke an operation without fixing how the programmer implements it. Once that boundary exists, the programmer can replace a prompt with code once a rule is clear, or swap code back to a prompt to test a changed requirement or relax an overly rigid rule. Unlike ordinary code-to-code information hiding, however, this boundary crosses two different execution regimes and serves both code and LLM callers, so the abstraction leaks asymmetrically in the two swap directions.

The [English account of prompting](./prompting-changes-failure-diagnosis-with-the-semantic-reference.md) treats an instruction as permitting a set of readings, from which an LLM executor produces one. It treats extracting a repeated operation into code as a separate intervention whose trade-off must be assessed. As a system evolves, components move in both directions across that boundary: recurring patterns move from prompts into code, and code moves back to prompts when requirements change or a coded rule proves too brittle. A unified interface is what makes that boundary movable without rewriting callers.

## The mechanism

Unifying code and prompts behind one interface requires three design choices:

- **Declared-argument call surface:** each callable receives only its declared arguments and returns a declared result format, rather than an agent implicitly inheriting the caller's full conversation history.
- **Dual-audience interface:** the same interface pairs a parameter and result schema (for code callers and boundary validation) with a natural-language description (for LLM callers).
- **Name-based binding:** callers invoke a string name, and the runtime resolves that name to either a prompt-backed agent or a function for the run.

[llm-do](https://github.com/zby/llm-do) illustrates this pattern: prompt-backed agents and Python functions share one callable namespace and invoke each other by name. Each callable receives only its declared arguments; an agent pairs its own system prompt with those declared arguments. The programmer binds a name such as `ticket_classifier` to either a prompt-backed agent or a Python function, and the runtime resolves the binding on each call. The programmer chooses the implementation for the run; the runtime does not decide ticket by ticket whether to use code or a model.

## What the interface hides and what leaks

Ordinary information hiding swaps two implementations that share the same execution substrate and caller model: changing a sorting algorithm or storage backend preserves the basic nature of a function call. Across the prompt–code boundary, a shared interface hides *how the rule is implemented*—avoiding call-site edits—but cannot hide *which execution regime handles the call*. Because both code and LLMs can act as callers, the two swap directions break different caller assumptions:

- **Prompt to code exposes loose LLM callers.** An LLM caller invokes an operation through its natural-language description as well as its schema. A prompt-backed callee often absorbs loosely phrased, slightly malformed, or context-dependent arguments by inferring intent. When the programmer replaces that prompt with strict code, the call signature stays identical, yet LLM callers that relied on that tolerance begin failing or triggering literal misreads. Enforcing input schemas strictly at the call boundary while the implementation is still a prompt prevents structural coupling—catching malformed arguments before code ever sees them—though schema-valid free-text arguments that rely on prompt interpretation still need caller testing after the swap.
- **Code to prompt exposes runtime assumptions in callers.** A signature does not express latency, token cost, determinism, or failure mode. A Python loop—or a budget-bound agent loop—that invokes a fast function repeatedly can multiply latency and token spend when that name is rebound to a prompt. Code written to catch deterministic exceptions can also break when a prompt-backed callee returns a model refusal, drifts across retries, or produces a schema-valid but wrong result.

The practical consequence is that interface parity alone is not enough for safe swapping. Call boundaries should enforce schemas before [codification](./definitions/codification.md) (moving a rule into symbolic form), and call sites that may move back to prompts must be written for fallible, higher-latency calls.

## Scope

- **Call invariance is not behavioral invariance:** What stays unchanged is the call, not its effect. A classifier with the same set of queue labels can still route a ticket to a different queue, so callers that relied on prior decisions or error behavior need testing after a swap.
- **Structural signature changes still require adapters:** If a new implementation requires structured arguments instead of free text, the call itself must change unless an adapter preserves the old interface.
- **Bidirectional swapping requires call-site headroom:** Moving code back to a prompt behind an unchanged call site works only where the caller's latency budget, cost budget, and error handling can absorb model execution; tight inner loops and hard deterministic paths do not qualify.

## Why this matters for constraining

[Constraining](./definitions/constraining.md) narrows the interpretation space, and [codification](./definitions/codification.md) moves a rule into symbolic form. In a system that exposes agents and tools through different invocation surfaces, moving a component between surfaces in either direction is a breaking change: call sites must be updated, prompt structure must change, and the agent's view of available operations shifts. This friction would likely discourage incremental changes and push toward big-bang rewrites. That effect is an expectation, not an observed result.

Suppose the team starts with a prompt for `ticket_classifier` while it learns how tickets should be assigned. The same unified binding then supports three distinct moves without editing callers:

- **Prompt to code (codification as refactoring).** By checking the agent's decisions against the queues that actually resolve the tickets, the team identifies a topic-based rule it wants to keep—[spec mining](./spec-mining-as-codification.md). If the team wants to preserve that chosen routing rule, replacing the prompt with a Python function changes the implementation rather than the rule, and the programmer rebinds `ticket_classifier` to the function.
- **Code to prompt for a changed requirement (prototyping).** Later the team wants to test routing tickets by the action the customer needs rather than by topic. The Python function still meets the old requirement. For a test run, the programmer binds `ticket_classifier` to a prompt instead, edits the prompt, and compares assignments on sample tickets without implementing each candidate policy in Python. Even if the winning rule goes back into code for production, the prompt let the team explore alternatives cheaply.
- **Code to prompt for [relaxing](./codification-and-relaxing-navigate-the-bitter-lesson-boundary.md) (regaining generality).** Separately, the team's goal may not have changed. Either the extracted Python rule proves to be a brittle proxy theory—an approximation that fails on edge cases or distribution shift—or a stronger, cheaper model now handles the broader task well enough ([relaxing signals](./operational-signals-that-a-component-is-a-relaxing-candidate.md)). Here rebinding `ticket_classifier` to a prompt reverses the earlier code extraction to recover generality, accepting higher runtime cost and variance.

Only the first move aims to preserve the chosen routing rule. Both code-to-prompt moves intentionally change behavior—one because the requirement changed, the other because the coded approximation proved too narrow. All three avoid call-site edits whenever callers stay within the boundary contract and can absorb the target execution regime.

## The connection to typed callables

[Instructions are typed callables](./instructions-are-typed-callables.md) argues that skills, tasks and workflows are callable in a limited sense: they take and return typed documents and can declare signatures, though a signature does not turn a natural-language procedure into a conventional function. This note extends that callable structure to tools. llm-do implements this pattern: `.agent` files are YAML frontmatter (type signature) plus system prompt (implementation), and tools are Python functions with type annotations. The unified interface is what makes this callable view practical across prompts and code rather than merely analogical.

## Open Questions

- How does a unified callable surface scale for LLM callers once hundreds of components exist, where tool-description selection degrades even when names are namespaced?
- How should tracing and error attribution work when a call chain alternates between prompts and code — do standard observability tools suffice, or does the boundary require dedicated trace semantics?
- Should a unified interface expose non-functional annotations (cost, latency, determinism) to callers, or does that re-expose the implementation detail the interface is meant to hide?

description: 'The title is phrased as a claim but only asserts a truism or a point nobody knowledgeable would contest.'
type: types/review-gate.md

## Failure mode

The title is phrased as a claim but only asserts a truism or a point nobody knowledgeable would contest.

## Test

Ask whether someone informed could reasonably argue the opposite. If not, the claim is weak.

Watch for **presupposed claims**: titles shaped like "`<hard noun phrase>` lets / enables / allows `<obvious consequence>`" smuggle the contestable claim into the subject and leave a near-truism as the main predicate. Ask whether the main verb asserts the hard point or assumes the subject already exists; if it assumes it, promote the presupposition into the main claim.

The fix is usually to sharpen the title to the non-obvious point the note actually establishes, or to switch to a topical title when the note is not making a contestable claim.

Topical titles remain valid for multi-claim specs, frameworks, definitional notes, indexes, and exploratory drafts.

## Example (fail)

- `continuous learning is substrate-independent`
- `validation should be fast`
- `a unified interface lets programmers choose prompts or code` *(presupposes prompts and code can share one interface; the predicate only restates what an interface does)*

## Example (pass)

- `continuous learning can happen outside of weights`
- `deterministic validation should be a script`
- `code and prompts can share a unified interface so programmers choose between them`

# Review result

A review result records one assessment of captured target text against a criterion. Completion means the output passed deterministic checks, not that its judgment is correct. A report outcome is not a favorable verdict. Use this type for individual gate, compression-check, type-conformance and collection-conformance verdicts, and for critique, composition-friction, premise-decomposition and compression-synthesis reports and role reports. Do not use it for combined improvement packets or connection discovery.

## Content

Findings state what the assessed text establishes or fails to establish. Each passage finding quotes enough verbatim text to identify one contiguous span uniquely. A quote is matched after whitespace and typographic quote marks are normalized, so a line wrap in the target does not break it. A quote therefore identifies a passage and is not a byte-exact copy of it. A consumer that needs the exact span locates the quote in the captured target, which holds the exact bytes. A document-wide or absence finding explains the condition without inventing a quotation. Finding levels belong to verdict criteria; critique reports instead state whether the strongest attack lands and how the note engages it. An empty findings list is an honest completed result when no finding remains.

The body explains the assessment without repeating every structured finding. A critique preserves its central commitment, critique mode, strongest case, the note's response and constructive findings, including why an attack does not survive. Low-confidence no-surviving-attack findings leave the need for a domain check visible.

Each report method has its own shape, which the schema checks by the result's `criterion`:

| Method | Findings | Required body |
|---|---|---|
| Critique | constructive findings | `attack-outcome` in frontmatter; `## Strongest case against it`, `## How the note engages it`, `## Constructive findings` |
| Composition friction | the surfaced joints, thinnest first; each reason begins `UNSUPPORTED`, `THIN` or `HOLDS` | a `**Filter:** SURVIVES` or `DISSOLVES` line; `## Filter`, `## Thinnest joints`, `## For the human` |
| Premise decomposition | one per premise; each reason begins `HOLDS`, `DOUBTFUL` or `DEFEATED`, and a non-`HOLDS` reason names `LOCAL` or `GLOBAL` and `instance`, `prevalence` or `priced-exception` | a `**Register:**` line; `## Premises and counterexamples`, `## For the human` |
| Compression synthesis | zero to three opportunities | `## Opportunities` |
| Role report | one per dependent need, duplication or untaken recommendation; each reason begins `SUPPLIED`, `PARTLY SUPPLIED`, `NOT SUPPLIED`, `DUPLICATED` or `UNTAKEN` | `## Role`, `## Dependents`, `## Duplication`, `## Untaken recommendations`, `## Reach` |

Only critique supplies `attack-outcome`. Friction's filter line and the premise statuses route attention; they are not overall verdicts. A report criterion is named by its library instruction's identity, so moving one of these instructions requires a schema edit.

## Field ownership

The worker fragment supplies only `type`, `findings`, `outcome`, optional `attack-outcome`, and the body. Findings precede the outcome so the serialized verdict follows its rationale. The fragment is not a complete saved artifact. The controller completes and validates it; workers never assert hashes, execution identities or timestamps.

| Fields | Owner and meaning |
|---|---|
| `type`, `findings`, `outcome`, `attack-outcome` | Worker assessment; findings contain `scope`, `quotes`, `reason`, and `level` for verdicts |
| `description`, `format`, `contract` | Controller's result-format identity and expected verdict/report contract |
| `note`, `criterion` | Original target and criterion identities |
| `note-sha256`, `criterion-sha256` | Freshness hashes; the note hash may cover normalized watched parts, not exact bytes |
| `target-sha256`, `target-capture` | Exact assessed UTF-8 bytes and their retained repository-relative location |
| `observation`, `contract-sha256` | Execution observation and captured output-contract identity |
| `profile`, `model`, `run`, `launch`, `completed-at` | Requested execution configuration and observed execution provenance |
| `raw-output`, `raw-output-sha256` | Retained original worker fragment, distinct from this completed artifact |

## Template

Worker fragment for a verdict criterion; code supplies the remaining fields:

```markdown
---
type: types/review-result.md
findings:
  - scope: document
    quotes: []
    reason: "The claim omits the condition needed for its stated conclusion."
    level: warn
outcome: warn
---

# Review

## Summary

The conclusion needs its missing condition.
```

A critique fragment uses `outcome: report`, supplies `attack-outcome`, and omits finding levels. Its body retains the critique instruction's sections. Other report fragments use `outcome: report`, omit `attack-outcome` and finding levels, and follow their instruction's Output section. Neither fragment uses a terminal `## Result:` line. Operational production and publication belong to the review command, not to this type.

# Writing conventions for kb/reports/ (report collection)

## Purpose and scope

This collection contains analytical outputs, evaluation records, and local
operational evidence that are consumed as reports rather than as library
claims or system definitions. Placement here is justified by the output's
retention policy and consumer, not by its filename or by the fact that a tool
generated it.

A report belongs here only when a named operation consumes the report itself.
Transferable claims belong in `kb/theory/`; descriptions of the shipped system
and its decisions belong in `kb/reference/`; executable procedures belong in
`kb/instructions/`; and reasoning whose value is consumed by unfinished work
belongs in `kb/work/`.

## Policy areas

Every report artifact lives in exactly one first-level policy area:

| Area | Retention policy | Typical contents |
|---|---|---|
| `state/` | Ignored, one directory per producing workflow. Not disposable merely because it was generated: the owning workflow decides when an output may be removed, and the [state README](./state/README.md) states per workflow what deletion loses. | Review results, packets and runs; fix dispositions; ingest working directories; connect, critique, friction, premise-decomposition and promotion-candidate reports. |
| `retained/` | Durable report records kept with the project. Payloads are tracked. | Evaluation corpora, experiment reports, measurements, and exact records cited by later work. |
| `types/` | Collection-local structural contracts, not report payloads. | Optional project-authored report contracts; command-produced generic report types are global. |

The published site includes `retained/` and leaves out `state/`. Inside `retained/`, a subtree carrying a
`.commonplace-validation-ignore` marker is left out of the site as well as
validation; mark exact captures and trial bundles so, keeping the report that
interprets them published.

Do not put report payloads directly at the collection root. Moving an artifact
between policy areas is a change in its retention contract, not a filing-only
rename.

## Quality goal

Make the report sufficient for the operation that consumes it without making
it impersonate a durable knowledge claim. State the subject, inputs or source
state, method, result, and material limits to the degree needed to interpret
or reproduce the output. Record the model and prompt or instruction identity
when an LLM judgment is part of the evidence and the producing workflow does
not already retain them.

`state/` must satisfy the owning workflow's authority, integrity, and cleanup
rules. `retained/` must remain
understandable from a clean checkout without relying on ignored files.

## Titles, descriptions, and exact records

- Use a title that names the analysis, experiment, or result. A title such as
  "Report" does not distinguish the artifact.
- When frontmatter is present, write a retrieval-oriented `description` that
  identifies the subject and why the exact output is retained.
- Frontmatter-free Markdown is permitted for deliberate unstructured output.
- Preserve an exact capture when fidelity is the report's purpose. If a copied
  artifact carries another collection's local type only as captured data, put
  a `.commonplace-validation-ignore` marker at the capture-set root rather than
  presenting that copy as a live typed artifact of this collection.

## Maintenance semantics

- A state producer owns cleanup and states, in the state README, what deleting
  its output loses: nothing unique (rebuild from retained inputs), one paid
  judgment (rerun when needed) or current coverage, an unresolved disposition
  or decision evidence (preserve). Generated state may contain non-reproducible
  judgments or the only current disposition, so Git ignore status never
  licenses deletion.
- A retained report is changed according to its declared role. Correct a
  living report in place; preserve a dated or frozen observation as an exact
  record and create a new observation when the measured state changes.
- Local evidence notes are the one interpreted form `retained/` keeps as
  durable artifacts: a `types/note.md` artifact whose bounded inference
  concerns only Commonplace's own choices or their measured effects, beside
  the raw records it interprets. Its formal edges use this collection's labels
  below. An inference that keeps a free variable belongs in
  `kb/theory/evidence/`.
- If a report develops a transferable claim, binding rule, system premise, or
  unfinished-work lifecycle, extract that content to its proper collection.
  Do not broaden `retained/` into a second notes, reference, instructions, or
  workshop collection.

## Outbound links

Reports may inspect any project surface. Use relative Markdown links for live
navigation and state in prose why the target matters. Inline links may carry
ordinary evidential or procedural context. Footer-shaped formal edges use this
small authorized set:

| label | destinations | reader need |
|---|---|---|
| `derived-from` | sources, external | inspect the source material from which the report was produced |
| `is-evidence-for` | theory, reference, reports | inspect the durable claim, decision, or report record on which this output bears |
| `compares-with` | theory, reference, sources, reports | compare two artifacts on a named shared axis |
| `see-also` | any durable collection, external | inspect useful adjacent context when no stronger relation applies |

The destination collection separately decides whether it may author a
reciprocal edge. A formal edge into this collection targets `retained/`;
`state/` may be mentioned inline only as local operational context.

Tracked library artifacts must not depend on an ignored `state/` file being
present. Summarize the needed evidence in the tracked artifact or
promote the exact report to `retained/` first. Tracked artifacts may cite a
`retained/` report when the exact record is useful to their reader.

## Validation markers

The tracked `.commonplace-validation-ignore` marker at `state/` excludes its
data-bearing subtree from collection-scoped validation. The marker does not
hide files from ordinary discovery, and explicit validation of
one typed report still applies its type contract.

A file under `state/` may declare any valid type spec, including another
collection's local type. Workflows stage candidates there for other
collections, and a candidate must validate against its destination's contract.
The type spec itself stays in the owning collection's `types/` directory.
`retained/` does not share this exception.

## What does not belong here

- A generated explanation or synthesis whose claim should survive the run →
  `kb/theory/` or `kb/reference/` according to its consumer.
- A procedure named "report" because it produces one → `kb/instructions/`.
- Drafts, deliberation, and run traces consumed by an unfinished investigation
  → `kb/work/`.
- External source captures and their durable analyses → `kb/sources/`.
- Build outputs with no report consumer → their build cache, not `kb/reports/`.
